usage: 내다 is the standard verb for paying out taxes, bills and fees; never 사다 or 주다
붙다 (to stick) is how Koreans say a tax or fee gets tacked onto a price
신고 申告 = official declaration; 종합소득세 신고 is the yearly income-tax filing
환급 還給 = money returned to you, e.g. the 연말정산 환급 at year-end
examples: 월급에서 세금이 자동으로 빠져요.
Tax comes out of my paycheck automatically.
에서 marks the source it leaves from; 빠지다 here = to be deducted
이 가격에 세금이 포함돼 있나요?
Is tax included in this price?
포함되다 = to be included; ask this when a quote looks suspiciously low
프리랜서는 세금을 직접 신고해야 돼요.
Freelancers have to file taxes themselves.
직접 = in person/by yourself; relevant for 3.3% 사업소득 work
nuance: 세금 is Sino-Korean 稅金, literally 'tax-money', the umbrella term covering income tax (소득세), VAT (부가세), property tax and the rest. The near-synonym to keep separate is 요금 料金, a usage charge or fare: your phone, gas and subway are 요금, while money owed to the government is 세금. Register is neutral and everyday; you 세금을 내다 (pay), and a tax can 붙다 (get stuck onto a price). The classic English-speaker trap is the verb: English 'buy' tempts learners into 세금을 사다, which is nonsense — tax is something you 내다, never 사다 or 주다. Also note 세금이 비싸다 sounds odd; Koreans say 세금이 많다/높다.

mistakes: Saying 세금을 사다 because English uses no special verb — you 내다 (pay out) tax, never 사다 (buy) or 주다 (give).
Calling your phone or electricity bill 세금 — a usage charge is 요금; 세금 is specifically money owed to the state.
Saying 세금이 비싸다 — prices are 비싸다, but a tax amount is described with 많다 or 높다: 세금이 많아요.

usage: The mandatory state pension 國民年金; foreigners on certain visas pay in too
받다 for the money you collect after retirement, not 사다 or 가지다
가입하다 + 에 is the verb for joining/signing up for any scheme
개인 個人 = personal; a voluntary retirement product from a bank or insurer
examples: 국민연금은 월급에서 매달 빠져나가요.
National pension is taken out of my salary every month.
빠져나가다 = to be withdrawn automatically; 매달 = every month
저는 노후를 위해 개인연금도 들었어요.
I also signed up for a private pension for my old age.
들다 (to sign up) is colloquial for joining insurance/pension; 노후 = later life
연금을 언제부터 받을 수 있어요?
From when can I start receiving the pension?
언제부터 = from when; a real question about payout age (now rising past 60)
nuance: 연금 is Sino-Korean 年金, literally 'year-money' — income paid out yearly/regularly in retirement. In daily speech it almost always means 국민연금, the compulsory national pension deducted from your pay; 개인연금 and 퇴직연금 (severance pension) are the extra products you choose yourself. The dangerous look-alike is 연봉 年俸 (annual salary): 연금 is retirement income while 연봉 is what you earn now, so swapping the two in a sentence is a real beginner slip. Register is neutral/official. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 연금 like any recurring 'monthly payment'; a subscription or installment is never 연금 — it specifically denotes old-age income. Foreigners can sometimes claim a lump-sum refund (반환일시금) on leaving Korea.

Saying 연금을 사다 — you 받다 (receive) a pension or 가입하다 (enroll), you never 'buy' it.

usage: 오르다 is the default verb; 물가가 올랐어요 is everyday small talk
the cost of living is high
Koreans treat overall prices as one thing that can be 비싸다
상승 上昇 = a rise; you'll see 물가 상승률 (inflation rate) in the news
안정되다 安定 = to become stable, the opposite of runaway inflation
examples: 요즘 물가가 너무 올라서 장 보기 무서워요.
Prices have risen so much lately that I'm scared to grocery shop.
장 보다 = to do grocery shopping; -아서 gives the reason
서울은 물가가 비싸지만 살기 편해요.
Seoul is expensive but convenient to live in.
-지만 = but; the standard way to describe a city's cost of living
월급은 그대로인데 물가만 올라요.
My salary stays the same but only prices keep rising.
그대로 = unchanged; -만 (only) highlights what is moving
nuance: 물가 is Sino-Korean 物價, literally 'thing-price' — the general price level of goods and services across the economy, not the tag on one item. That is exactly where it splits from its near-synonyms 가격 價格 and 값: 가격/값 is the price of a single product, while 물가 is the aggregate cost of living. So '이 물가가 비싸요' about one coffee is wrong; you mean 가격 or 값. When friends gripe about inflation they say 물가가 올랐다, never 가격이 다 올랐다. Register is fully casual and it is one of the most-used money words in Korea right now. Pronunciation trap: the 가 is tensed (sounds like mulkka) but is still spelled 가, so don't write 물까.

mistakes: Saying 이 물가가 비싸요 about a single product — use 가격 or 값 for one item's price; 물가 is only the overall price level.
Spelling it 물까 or 물카 because of the tense pronunciation — it is always 물가.
Using 물가 for an exchange rate or stock — 물가 is consumer prices; market quotes are 시세 and rates are 환율/금리.

usage: When 환율 rises the won is weaker — costlier to buy dollars, but good for incoming foreign cash
확인하다 確認 — what you do before remitting or exchanging cash
좋다 here means favorable for you specifically, not high
우대 優待 = a discount on the spread your bank or app offers
examples: 오늘 환율이 좋아서 본국으로 송금했어요.
The rate was good today so I sent money home.
송금 = remittance; -아서 links the good rate to the action
환율 때문에 해외 직구가 비싸졌어요.
Overseas online shopping got expensive because of the exchange rate.
때문에 = because of; 해외 직구 = direct overseas purchase
달러 환율이 1,400원을 넘었어요.
The dollar exchange rate passed 1,400 won.
넘다 = to exceed; numbers like this come up constantly in 2020s Korea
nuance: 환율 is Sino-Korean 換率, literally 'exchange-rate' (換 swap + 率 ratio) — the price of one currency in terms of another, central to anyone who remits money or shops abroad. The crucial near-synonym to separate is 환전 換錢, 'exchanging the actual cash': 환율 is the rate, 환전 is the act of swapping money at that rate, so you 환전하다 at a given 환율. Register is neutral. Two pitfalls bite English speakers: first, 환율이 좋다 means favorable-for-you, not numerically high; second, English makes 'the rate went up' sound positive, but 환율이 올랐다 means the foreign currency got more expensive in won, so sending money home actually costs you more. Watch for 환율 우대 (rate discount) on bank and Wise/Toss apps.

mistakes: Confusing 환율 (the exchange rate) with 환전 (the act of changing cash) — you 환전하다 your money at a 환율; the rate itself is never 환전.
Assuming 환율이 올랐다 is good news — a higher won-per-dollar rate means dollars cost more, so remittances and overseas shopping get pricier.
Reading 환율이 좋다 as 'high' — it means favorable to you, which for a buyer of foreign currency is actually a lower rate.

usage: 붙다 (to stick) is the natural verb — your savings earn 이자가 붙어요
내다 when you owe it, e.g. on a loan: 대출 이자를 내다
율 率 = rate; the more formal/news word is 금리 金利
높다/낮다 describe the amount — great for savings, painful for loans
examples: 이 적금은 이자가 높은 편이에요.
This installment savings account has relatively high interest.
적금 = installment savings; -은 편이다 = on the higher side
대출 이자가 매달 나가서 부담돼요.
The loan interest goes out every month and it's a burden.
부담되다 = to feel like a financial burden; 나가다 = to go out (be paid)
요즘 금리가 올라서 이자가 늘었어요.
Rates went up lately so the interest increased.
Note 금리 (the rate) drives 이자 (the actual money); 늘다 = to increase
nuance: 이자 is Sino-Korean 利子, literally 'profit-child' — money that 'breeds' from a sum, i.e. the actual won your savings earn or that you owe on a loan. The line to draw is 이자 (the money) versus 이자율 / 금리 (the rate, a percentage): 금리가 3%면 이자가 3만 원 — the rate produces the interest. Register is everyday. Whether 이자 is welcome depends entirely on your side of the table: 예금 이자 (deposit interest) is income you 받다, while 대출 이자 (loan interest) is a cost you 내다. The English-speaker pitfall is double: don't use 이자 for the percentage (that's 이자율/금리), and don't say 이자를 받다 about a loan you owe — you only 받다 interest on your own deposits; on a loan you 내다.

Saying 이자를 받다 about a loan you took out — you 내다 (pay) loan interest; you 받다 (receive) interest only on your own savings.
Treating 이자 and 금리 as fully interchangeable — 금리 is the abstract rate (used in news/policy), 이자 is the concrete money on your account.

usage: 갚다 = to pay back a debt; loan repayment is 원금 + 이자
보장 保障 = guarantee; the key phrase separating safe from risky products
손실 損失 = loss; the risk warning on funds and stocks
The two parts of any loan or deposit payout
examples: 이 상품은 원금이 보장돼요.
This product guarantees your principal.
보장되다 = to be guaranteed; reassuring for cautious savers
주식은 원금 손실 위험이 있어요.
Stocks carry the risk of losing your principal.
위험이 있다 = there is a risk; standard disclaimer for new investors
매달 원금이랑 이자를 같이 갚고 있어요.
I'm repaying the principal and interest together every month.
-이랑 = casual 'and'; 같이 = together
nuance: 원금 is Sino-Korean 元金, literally 'origin-money' — the original sum you deposited or borrowed, kept separate from the 이자 (interest) layered on top. The pairing 원금 vs 이자 is the backbone of every loan and savings calculation. Beware the look-alike 현금 現金 (cash on hand): they share 金 but 원금 is a principal balance, not physical money. Register is neutral, common in bank apps and contracts. The most damaging English-speaker misreading is 원금 보장 (principal protected): it guarantees only that you won't lose your initial amount — it does NOT promise any profit. So a 펀드 that is not 원금 보장 can drop below what you put in (원금 손실), which is precisely the warning attached to 주식 and 펀드.

Saying 원금을 내다 for repaying a loan — you 갚다 (pay back) the principal of a debt; 내다 fits taxes and fees, not loan principal.

usage: to sign up for a fund
가입하다 + 에 — the verb for buying into a fund at a bank/app
투자하다 投資 = to invest; the general action, also takes 에
수익률 收益率 = rate of return; what you check to see if you're up or down
적립식 積立式 = paying a fixed amount monthly, popular for beginners
examples: 은행에서 펀드를 추천받았는데 좀 고민돼요.
The bank recommended a fund but I'm a bit torn.
추천받다 = to get recommended; -는데 sets up the hesitation that follows
저는 매달 조금씩 펀드에 넣고 있어요.
I put a little into a fund each month.
넣다 (to put in) + 에 is the everyday verb for contributing money
펀드는 원금을 잃을 수도 있어요.
With a fund you could lose your principal.
-(으)ㄹ 수도 있다 = it's possible that; links back to 원금
nuance: 펀드 is a loanword from English 'fund' (write 펀드, never 펀트), meaning a pooled investment product — a mutual fund you buy through a bank app or securities account. The defining contrast is with 예금/적금 (bank deposit/installment savings): those are 원금 보장 with fixed 이자, whereas a 펀드 has no guaranteed return and your 원금 is genuinely at risk. Note also 펀드 vs 주식 株式 (individual stocks): a 펀드 is a managed basket, 주식 is buying one company directly. Register is neutral, very common among 20–30s who start with an 적립식 펀드 before moving to 주식/ETF on apps like 토스증권 or 키움. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming a 펀드 behaves like a savings account — it does not; returns can be negative, so you 잃다 (lose), not just earn.

usage: 쓰다 (to write) is the set verb — 가계부 쓰다 = to track spending, not 만들다
Most people now use a 가계부 앱 like 뱅크샐러드 instead of paper
to tidy up / review the budget
정리하다 整理 = to organize, e.g. at month's end
to write down in the budget
적다 = to jot down each expense; takes 에 for the place written into
examples: 이번 달부터 가계부를 쓰기 시작했어요.
I started keeping a budget this month.
-부터 = starting from; -기 시작하다 = to begin doing
가계부를 보니까 배달 음식에 돈을 너무 많이 썼어요.
Looking at my budget, I spent way too much on delivery food.
-(으)니까 here = upon doing and discovering; 배달 음식 = delivery food
저는 가계부 앱으로 카드 내역을 자동으로 관리해요.
I manage my card history automatically with a budgeting app.
-(으)로 = by means of; 내역 = transaction history
nuance: 가계부 is Sino-Korean 家計簿, literally 'household-finance ledger' (家 home + 計 reckoning + 簿 register), but today it almost always means a budgeting app that auto-syncs your cards and accounts. The fixed collocation is 가계부를 쓰다 (write/keep), so 가계부를 만들다 sounds off for daily tracking — that would imply building the ledger itself. Don't confuse the 가계부 (your running budget) with its inputs: a 영수증 領收證 is one receipt and a 명세서 明細書 is a statement, both of which feed into the 가계부. Register is casual and warm; keeping one is a classic money-saving habit, especially when people see how much goes to 배달 and 카페. It pairs naturally with 지출 and 절약.

usage: to build up an emergency fund
모으다 = to gather/save up over time, bit by bit
to dip into the emergency fund
쓰다 when an emergency finally forces you to use it
숨기다 = to hide; jokingly, money kept secret from a partner
통장 通帳 = bankbook/account; a separate one kept just for emergencies
examples: 갑자기 병원비가 나와서 비상금을 썼어요.
I had a sudden hospital bill so I used my emergency fund.
병원비 = medical costs; 나오다 here = (a bill) comes up
매달 조금씩 비상금을 모으고 있어요.
I'm saving up a little emergency money each month.
조금씩 = little by little; -고 있다 = ongoing habit
비상금은 따로 통장에 넣어 두세요.
Keep your emergency fund in a separate account.
따로 = separately; -어 두다 = do in advance and leave it that way
nuance: 비상금 is Sino-Korean 非常金, literally 'non-ordinary money' (非常 emergency + 金 money) — cash set aside for the unexpected: a sudden 병원비, job loss, a broken phone. It carries a fun second life too: secret stash money hidden from a spouse, a staple gag in dramas and memes. The contrast to nail is 비상금 vs 용돈 (allowance / spending money): 용돈 is for everyday spending and is meant to be used up, while 비상금 stays untouched until a real emergency. Register is casual. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 비상금 like investment money — the whole point is that it stays safe and instantly accessible (in a 통장, not a 펀드), so it should NOT be exposed to 원금 손실. Finance content for 20–30s always says build a 비상금 first.

Sino-Korean 非常金, literally 'non-ordinary money' (非常 emergency + 金 money).
The pitfall is treating 비상금 like investment money — the whole point is that it stays safe and instantly accessible (in a 통장, not a 펀드), so it should NOT be exposed to 원금 손실.

mistakes: Confusing 비상금 (untouched emergency savings) with 용돈 (allowance for everyday spending) — 용돈 is meant to be spent, 비상금 is reserved for emergencies.
Treating 비상금 as investment money — its purpose is safety and instant access, so it belongs in a 통장, not a risky 펀드.
Saying 비상금을 내다 — you 모으다 (save up) or 쓰다 (use) emergency money; 내다 is for paying taxes and fees.

usage: 늘다/줄다 for income going up or down; not 오르다 for income itself
세 稅 = tax; the tax levied specifically on your 소득
증명 證明 = proof; 소득 증명서 is needed for visas, loans, leases
고정 固定 = fixed; a regular salary vs. irregular freelance income
examples: 대출을 받으려면 소득 증명이 필요해요.
You need proof of income to take out a loan.
-(으)려면 = if you want to; also required for some visa renewals
부업으로 소득을 조금 늘렸어요.
I increased my income a bit with a side job.
부업 = side job; -(으)로 = by means of; the side-hustle trend is big
소득이 일정하지 않아서 저축이 어려워요.
My income isn't steady so saving is hard.
일정하다 = to be regular/consistent; -지 않다 = negation
nuance: 소득 is Sino-Korean 所得, literally 'that which is obtained' (所 that-which + 得 gain) — the formal word for income or earnings used in official contexts: taxes (소득세), loan and visa paperwork (소득 증명), statistics. It covers ALL earnings, not just salary — freelance, rental and investment income are equally 소득. The near-synonyms to separate are 월급 月給 (your monthly paycheck, what people say in casual chat) and 수익 收益 (profit/return on something invested): 소득 is your total earned income, while 수익 implies a gain produced by an investment. Register is formal/documentary; in everyday talk people just say 월급, switching to 소득 the moment documents or taxes appear. It is the natural counterpart to 지출.

Saying 소득이 올랐다 — income goes 늘다 (increases) or 줄다 (decreases); 오르다 fits prices (물가) and rates, not income.

usage: 줄이다 = to reduce; the core money-saving move
고정 固定 = fixed; rent, 관리비, subscriptions that recur each month
많다/적다 to describe how much you spend, not 비싸다
내역 內譯 = itemized record, what a 가계부 app shows you
examples: 이번 달은 지출이 너무 많았어요.
I spent way too much this month.
이번 달 = this month; 많다 describes the amount of spending
고정 지출부터 줄여 보세요.
Try cutting your fixed expenses first.
-부터 = starting from; -어 보다 = give it a try
수입과 지출을 비교해 봤어요.
I compared my income and spending.
수입과 지출 (income and spending) is the very common fixed pairing
nuance: 지출 is Sino-Korean 支出, literally 'pay-out' (支 disburse + 出 go-out) — money flowing out, your spending or expenses, and the natural opposite of 소득/수입. Budgeting talk constantly contrasts 수입 vs 지출, and the first advice is always 고정 지출 (fixed costs) 줄이기. Two distinctions matter: the everyday pairing is 수입과 지출 (not 소득과 지출, which sounds technical), and 지출 (money you spend) must not be confused with the look-alike 지급 支給 (a payment being issued/disbursed, usually by an institution to someone). Register is mildly formal but completely normal in money conversations; it feels a notch more precise than just 돈을 쓰다. The English-speaker pitfall is describing it with 비싸다 — spending is 많다/적다 (high/low in amount), never 비싸다.

usage: Add 하다 to make it a verb; 전기를 절약하다 = save electricity
Seen on appliances and public-campaign signs; 절약 isn't only about money
정신 精神 = spirit/mindset; praising someone's frugal habits
절약 covers time too — 시간 절약 = time-saving
examples: 요즘 돈을 아끼려고 외식을 줄이고 절약하고 있어요.
Lately I'm cutting eating out and economizing to save money.
아끼다 = to use sparingly; -(으)려고 = in order to
전기를 절약하면 관리비가 줄어요.
If you save electricity, your maintenance fee goes down.
-(으)면 = if; 관리비 = building maintenance fee
대중교통을 이용하면 교통비를 절약할 수 있어요.
Using public transport lets you save on transport costs.
교통비 = transport expenses; -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 = to be able to
nuance: 절약 is Sino-Korean 節約, literally 'to moderate and bind' (節 temperance + 約 restrain) — deliberate, sensible economizing, turned into a verb with 하다 (절약하다). It applies to money, energy and time alike and carries a positive, virtuous tone: being good at 절약 is a compliment. Two contrasts clarify it. First, 절약 vs 저축 貯蓄: 절약 is spending less in the first place, while 저축 is putting money aside into savings — you 절약해서 저축한다. Second, 절약 vs 인색 吝嗇 (stinginess): 절약 is admirable thrift, but 인색하다 or 짠돌이 is the negative 'cheapskate' sense. Register is positive and everyday; it pairs with 아끼다 (use sparingly) and is the goal behind keeping a 가계부. The English-speaker pitfall is using 절약 to mean 'stingy' — that crosses into 인색, a different, unflattering word.
